title: Bill Division (Bon Appétit)
directAnswer: Anna refuses to pay for one item she did not eat. Her fair share is half of the bill minus that one item: (total − bill[k]) / 2. If the amount Brian charged her, b, equals that fair share, print "Bon Appetit"; otherwise she was overcharged and you print the refund b − fairShare. Summing the bill is O(n).

remember.pattern: Sum, subtract the skipped item, halve, compare
remember.formula:
total = sum(bill)
fair = (total - bill[k]) // 2
print("Bon Appetit" if fair == b else b - fair)
rules: **Exclude item k before halving**, not after: fair share is `(total − bill[k]) / 2`, the cost split of everything Anna actually shared.
The two split the **non-k items equally**, so each owes half of `total − bill[k]`.
If the charged amount `b` equals the fair share, print **exactly** `"Bon Appetit"` — string match, capital B and A.
Otherwise the refund is `b − fair`, always **non-negative** here because Anna can only be overcharged for the item she skipped.
Integer division is safe — the problem guarantees `total − bill[k]` is even so the split is exact.
whenToUse: Split a total fairly after removing specific items
Compare an actual charge against a computed expected value
Any 'who owes what' after one party opts out of a line item
A single linear pass to total then a constant-time adjustment
antiSignals: Multiple opted-out items with different owners → track per-person sums
Uneven or weighted splits → not a plain halving
You need running totals over queries → prefix sums
Tax / tip percentages layered on → more arithmetic than one subtraction
remember.takeaway: Fair-share problems are: total everything, remove what doesn't apply, divide by the number of payers, then compare to what was charged. Bon Appétit is the two-person, one-skipped-item case — (total − bill[k]) / 2 versus b.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you compute a fair split by removing the excluded item before halving, and correctly branch between the exact-charge ('Bon Appetit') and overcharge (print refund) cases — simple arithmetic with an easy off-by-one in the order of operations.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Halving the full total and then subtracting, or subtracting bill[k] after dividing, both of which compute the wrong fair share. Also printing the wrong string casing.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the fair share as 'half of everything except item k', compute it in one pass, and note the refund is b − fairShare only when they differ.

problemStatement:
Anna and Brian are sharing a meal and splitting the bill, but Brian forgot that Anna did not eat item `k`. The cost of each item is given in an array `bill`.

Anna's fair share is half the cost of everything **except** item `k`. Brian charged Anna `b`.

If `b` equals Anna's fair share, print `"Bon Appetit"`. Otherwise, Anna was overcharged — print the difference `b − fairShare`, the amount Brian owes her back.
constraints: 0 ≤ k < n (index of the item Anna did not eat)
total − bill[k] is even, so the split is exact
b is the amount Anna was actually charged
understanding: Anna pays half of the cost of every item she actually shared, which is every item except item k. So her fair share is (sum of all items − bill[k]) / 2. Compare that to what Brian charged her, b. Equal means he split it correctly; larger means he charged her for the item she skipped, and the overpayment is b − fairShare.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the cost of the skipped item removed before or after dividing?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Before. Anna shares everything except item k, so her share is (total − bill[k]) / 2 — subtract first, then halve.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the refund be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Anna can only be overcharged (for the item she skipped) or charged correctly, so b − fairShare is always ≥ 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What exact string is expected when the charge is fair?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: "Bon Appetit" — that exact capitalisation and spelling. A mismatch fails the check.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the division guaranteed to be exact?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The problem guarantees total − bill[k] is even, so integer division gives the precise half with no rounding.

examples.explanation: Total = 24, minus item k (10) = 14, fair share = 7. Brian charged 12, so the refund is 12 − 7 = 5.
Fair share is 7 and Brian charged exactly 7 — no refund needed.
Total = 4, minus item 0 (2) = 2, fair share = 1, matches the charge.

approaches.name: Skip-in-Loop — Sum Everything Except k
approaches.whenToMention: A clear first pass: add up costs while skipping index k, then halve. Mention it, then note the branchless variant.
hints: Anna shares every item except item k, so add up all costs whose index is not k.
Halve that sum to get her fair share, since she and Brian split it evenly.
Compare to b: equal prints "Bon Appetit", otherwise print the overpayment b − fairShare.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n items with a constant-time check each, plus a few arithmetic operations — O(n) time, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build Anna's share directly by summing only the items she actually shared.

**The split model.** Anna and Brian divide the cost of the shared items equally. The shared items are everything except item `k`, the one Anna did not eat. So Anna's fair share is half the sum of all costs at indices other than `k`.

**Summing with a skip.** Walk the array and add `bill[i]` whenever `i != k`. That excludes the skipped item as you go, leaving the total cost of shared items. Halving it gives Anna's fair contribution.

**Deciding the output.** Compare the fair share with what Brian charged, `b`. If they are equal, the split was correct and the answer is the literal string `"Bon Appetit"`. If `b` is larger, Brian mistakenly charged Anna for the skipped item; the amount he owes her back is `b − fairShare`.

**Why a tiny refinement helps.** The per-iteration `if (i != k)` check is harmless but slightly noisy. The optimal variant drops it by summing everything and subtracting `bill[k]` once — the same result with a cleaner loop. Either is O(n); mention the skip version, then show the subtraction version.
approaches.insight: Skipping index k inside the loop and subtracting bill[k] after a full sum compute the same fair share. Seeing that equivalence is the small 'can we simplify the loop?' observation interviewers like.

approaches.name: Total Minus Item — Branchless Sum (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The clean answer: sum everything once, subtract bill[k], halve. No per-element branch.
hints: Sum the whole array first — no condition in the loop.
Subtract the skipped item's cost once after the loop: total − bill[k].
Halve to get the fair share, then compare to b for the same two outcomes.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single clean pass to total the array, then constant-time subtraction, halving, and comparison — O(n) time, O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Same result, simpler loop: total everything, then remove the one item.

**Why the branch comes out of the loop.** Instead of testing `i != k` on every iteration, sum the entire bill unconditionally, then subtract `bill[k]` exactly once. The arithmetic is identical — `(total − bill[k])` is the cost of the shared items — but the inner loop is now a plain sum, which is easier to read and reason about.

**Computing the fair share.** Halve `total − bill[k]`. The problem guarantees this quantity is even, so integer division is exact and there is no rounding to worry about.

**The two outcomes.** If the fair share equals what Brian charged (`b`), print `"Bon Appetit"`. Otherwise Anna was overcharged by `b − fairShare`, and that difference is the refund. Because Anna can only ever be charged the correct amount or be overcharged for item `k`, the difference is never negative.

**Why this is the version to write.** It separates the two concerns cleanly — one pass to total, one line to adjust — and avoids re-checking the same constant index n times. Functionally equal to the skip-in-loop version, just tidier.
approaches.insight: Subtracting bill[k] once after a full sum is the branchless twin of skipping it inside the loop. The fair share is 'cost of everything shared, split two ways' — the order is sum, subtract, halve, compare.

edgeCases.behavior: total = 0, fair = (0 − 0)/2 = 0, b = 0 → Bon Appetit. Zero-cost items are fine.
total = 20, fair = (20 − 5)/2 = 7 (given even-guarantee inputs this case wouldn't arise); with valid data fair matches or refund prints.

pitfalls: Computing fair as total/2 − bill[k] instead of (total − bill[k])/2.
Subtracting bill[k] after halving, which double-discounts the item.

commonMistakes: Halving the full total before removing the skipped item, giving the wrong fair share.
Forgetting to exclude item k, so Anna is charged for what she didn't eat.
Printing the wrong string when the charge is fair (casing or spelling).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong order of operations
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Anna's share is half of (total − bill[k]). Halving first, or subtracting bill[k] after halving, both miscompute it.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int fair = total / 2 - bill[k];   // double-discounts the item
commonMistakesDetailed.good: int fair = (total - bill[k]) / 2; // remove item, then split

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not excluding item k
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you sum the whole bill and halve, Anna pays for the item she skipped — the entire point of the problem.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: fair = sum(bill) // 2          # includes the skipped item

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong output string
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The checker expects exactly 'Bon Appetit'. Variants like 'bon appetit' or printing 0 fail.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: print("Bon Appetit")           # exact string on a fair charge
